This is the last working session on Whodunit before the neatHack cutoff. Submissions open today, Monday 12 October 2026, at 7:00 PM IST and are planned to close at 11:55 PM IST. Check the clock with `TZ=Asia/Kolkata date` before you start and after each job, and stop starting new work at 11:00 PM so there is time to test, commit and push.

Read `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, the last five entries of `hackathon.md`, and `evidence/README.md` before changing anything. `AGENTS.md` still governs: this session is recorded by Entire and will be public, keys stay in `.env` and are never printed, and pushing, posting, opening pull requests and writing to cfo.ai are my steps, which you ask me for. Where this message and `AGENTS.md` disagree, ask me.

## Why this session exists

I had the repo reviewed against the hackathon's rubric (the agent 30%, use of neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai 25%, demo video 20%, building in public 15%, usefulness and originality 10%). The review's findings, which I agree with:

1. A first-time reader cannot tell what Whodunit is for. The README opens with a riddle and then explains statistics. The outcome, a refund agent paying strangers and the one commit behind it, is four paragraphs down.
2. Everything is measured on a refund agent whose history I grew myself. Nothing shows it working on a history somebody else wrote.
3. It reads as a search algorithm with a model on the side. The loop that opens a case from a trace, writes a patch, throws out a patch that harms other requests, retries, reverts, and leaves a case open is real, but the README does not show it as one loop.
4. Nothing in the product reads the cfo.ai plan. The plan is a document beside the code.
5. The failing and passing runs each case cites are in local neatroots only, so nobody else can open them.
6. The README links none of my public posts.

The jobs below are in priority order. Do them in this order, finish each before starting the next, and tell me when one is done. If a job is blocked for more than twenty minutes, write down what blocked it and move on.

## Rules for every job

- Every number that goes into the README, a case page or a post comes from a record file or a run you made in this session. Check it against the file before you write it. If two files disagree, tell me; do not pick one.
- Report misses as plainly as hits. If the outside run names the wrong commit or names nobody, that goes in the write-up as it happened. This repo's habit of saying what went wrong is one of its strengths and I want it kept.
- Do not write anything addressed to the hackathon's judges, by name or as a group, and do not write text meant for automated graders.
- Do not rewrite git history. Do not wire the two-change-point model into the lineup tonight.
- Append a dated entry to `hackathon.md` after each job, in the style of the existing ones: what was done, what went wrong, what was not checked.
- Model spend: the last build-log estimate put the hackathon gateway at about $16 of $20. Before any job that makes model calls, estimate its cost, tell me, and stop at the cap I give you. Ask me if a job needs my own key instead.

## Job 1: the first screen of the README (about 45 minutes)

Rewrite the top of `README.md` so that a reader knows within ten seconds what broke, what Whodunit found, and what that is worth. Lead with the outcome and put the method after it. Here is the shape I want. Check each number against `cases/whole-history.record.json` and `evidence/README.md` and correct any that are off. The "11 minutes" comes from `pitch/demo-script.md`; confirm it from the record or a log, and drop it if you cannot.

```markdown
# Whodunit

Your AI agent worked last week. Now it gets things wrong, sometimes.
Whodunit tells you which change broke it, who asked for that change, and what it cost.

**One real case, one command, 11 minutes, about 80 cents:**

| | |
|---|---|
| What went wrong | A refund agent started refunding orders to people who did not own them. 11 of 14 runs. |
| Which change | 1 commit out of 57, named at 98.3% after 20 replays |
| Who asked for it | A coding-agent session where someone typed "simple refunds feel slow". Quoted from the Entire checkpoint. |
| What it cost | 120.00 refunded to the wrong people (test shop, scripted customers) |
| The fix | First patch passed 30 replays, broke another request, and was thrown out. Second patch kept: 0 failures in 30. |

Without it, someone reads traces and diffs for an afternoon, and `git bisect` cannot help
because the bug does not fail every time.
```

Under that, in this order:

- `evidence/lineup-whole-history.png`, with a link to the live case page at https://kinnuworks.github.io/whodunit/whole-history.casefile.html.
- A section called "What it does on its own" that shows the loop as one run: a case opened from a single failing trace, the lineup, the motive, the brief, my one ruling, a patch, the do-no-harm check, the retry, the revert when patches fall short, and a case left open when nothing clears the bar. Point each step at the case record where it actually happened (`whole-history`, `turned-away`, `half-done-batch`).
- A table called "Evidence" with one row for each of these and one link each: a before and after with numbers; neatlogs traces or screenshots; Entire checkpoints; the cfo.ai plan with its read-only share link (it is in `evidence/README.md` today); a run where an action failed and what happened next; public posts; commits dated inside the hackathon.
- In the posts row, these three, which are live:
  - https://x.com/heykinnu/status/2108892698963071343 (Day 1, 10 October)
  - https://x.com/heykinnu/status/2109010623833297271 (Bingo, 11 October)
  - https://x.com/heykinnu/status/2109552985152119291 (the pitch, 12 October)
  I will post more through the evening and paste the links to you. Add each one to the README and to `evidence/README.md`, which still lists post links as missing.
- "Why plain bisect is not enough" and everything else that is in the README now, unchanged in substance, below all of this.

Then make the same opening sentence ("Your AI agent worked last week...") the first line of the casebook index, by changing the casebook template under `whodunit/casefile/` and running `uv run whodunit casebook`. Update the one-line pitch in `AGENTS.md` to match, keeping "which commit, and why" first as that file requires. Give me the text for the GitHub repo description; I will set it.

## Job 2: one history I did not write (time box: two and a half hours)

This is the most valuable job and the riskiest. The aim is one honest result on a repository whose history, regressions and coding sessions are somebody else's.

The target is https://github.com/jaxsonsprinkles/support-agent-demo, a public customer-support agent built by another neatHack team as the demo target for their own tool. Its README says its history carries three seeded regressions. It has 30 commits, a CLI (`python -m agent "<question>"` prints the reply and tool calls as JSON), and `evals/cases.jsonl` with 24 cases, each with an input and checks such as `must_call`, `must_not_call`, `call_args` and `reply_contains`.

I approve cloning and reading that one public repository at a path outside this repo, for example `/tmp/outside/support-agent-demo`. That is the only exception to the rule in `AGENTS.md` about files outside the repo. It has no licence file, so do not copy any of its code or data into this repo. Link it and credit its author by name.

Keep the run blind, the way `eval/sealed` was:

- Use the range from `1b40b27` (good) to `0ecffc0` (bad), the tip of `main`.
- The team that built it publishes an answer key in their other repository, `jaxsonsprinkles/agentbisect`. Do not open that repository, and do not read `support-agent-demo` history from before `1b40b27`, until step 5 below.

Steps:

1. Work out the smallest change that lets Whodunit run a case against a foreign agent with `--repo`. Today a case's check is the list of refunds the agent printed. A general check is needed: tools that must be called, tools that must not be called, call arguments, and text the reply must contain, read from the JSON the agent prints. Build that as a proper check type with tests, since it also removes a limit the README admits (damages and checks tied to the refund agent).
2. Find out how to give that agent a model. It uses the Anthropic API with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and a pinned small model. Try the hackathon gateway through environment variables only, without editing the target. If that cannot work, stop and ask me for a key. Estimate the cost of the whole job first.
3. Write two or three case files under `cases/outside/`, each from one of that repo's own eval cases, chosen so the checks pass at the good ref and fail at the bad one. Let the lineup's own check of both ends confirm that. Pick cases from different categories so they can point at different commits.
4. Run `whodunit lineup` on each, with the statistical bisect and the usual 95% bar. Then run the motive step. That repo's commits carry Entire checkpoint trailers, but its checkpoint branch does not appear to be published, so expect the motive to fall back to the commit message. Say so on the page if it does.
5. Write the named culprits, their probabilities and the replay counts to `eval/outside/predictions.json` and commit it. Only then open `agentbisect/evidence/ground_truth.json` and any notes beside it, and score the predictions.
6. Write `eval/outside/README.md`: whose repo it is and that the regressions are theirs, what Whodunit named, what the key says, replays and spend per case, anything it got wrong or could not decide, and what had to change in Whodunit to run a foreign agent. Generate the case pages and add them to the casebook under their own heading.
7. Add one row to the README's top table or just under it: the outside result in one line, with a link.

Do not run the fix step on the outside repo. Naming the commit is the point.

If there is no successful replay of that agent after sixty minutes, stop, write up what blocked it in `hackathon.md`, and go to Job 3. A written-up attempt is worth more than a rushed result I cannot stand behind.

## Job 3: neatlogs evidence other people can open (about 40 minutes)

- `neatroots cloud login` is my step. Ask me to run it. Then push the failing run and the passing run that each case's brief cites to neatlogs cloud.
- Ask me for the dashboard address of one trace so `NEATLOGS_TRACE_URL` can be set, then rerun `uv run whodunit casebook` so each case page links its cited runs. Remove the sentence on each page that says the runs are in neatroots only, once it is no longer true.
- Turn the headline case into a standing check: a neatlogs detection that fires when `issue_refund` runs with no earlier `lookup_order` in the same run. Preview it against the recorded runs and record how many it flags before and after the fix commit. Put the detection id and the counts in `evidence/README.md`. Tell me what to screenshot.
- If `whodunit onset --cloud` can open a case from that detection, show that once and record the command and its output.

## Job 4: the cfo.ai plan sets a limit in code (about an hour)

Today no code reads the plan. Change that in the smallest honest way.

- With my yes, read these from the cfo.ai model: the price of the Team tier, the investigations it includes if the plan states that, the modelled cost of one investigation, and the target margin. Write them to `pitch/plan.json` with the date and the share link. Reading is fine; write nothing to cfo.ai.
- Derive one number from the file: the most a single investigation may spend on replays and model calls if the plan's margin is to hold. Put the formula in a comment and in the README.
- `whodunit investigate` takes that as its default spend limit, counted with the same token-cost estimate `damages.py` already uses. When a case reaches the limit it stops the way it stops today when replays run out: nobody is named below 95% and the lineup is handed back with its probabilities. A flag can raise the limit, and the case record says when it was raised.
- Add tests: the limit is read from the file, a run that would cross it stops, and the record says why.
- Check the six existing cases against the limit and say in the README which of them would have been stopped. If `half-done-batch`, at $3.53 of replays, is over it, say so. That is an honest and useful result.

## Job 5: the video's first ten seconds (propose only)

I have not asked you to rebuild the film. Read `pitch/demo-script.md` and what is in `pitch/video/`, and tell me:

- whether the first ten seconds say what broke and what Whodunit is for, in the words of the new README opening;
- whether the film shows any real terminal output or real case page, or only drawn screens;
- the smallest change that would fix either, and what it would cost in narration characters.

Change nothing in the film until I say so.

## Job 6: the submission

Write `pitch/submission.md` with the text for my submission post: team, name, project, public repo, demo link, the casebook link, and the three sponsor handles as I used them in my Day 1 post. Under 280 characters. Leave the demo link as a blank for me to fill.

## Before every push

1. `uv run pytest -m "not slow"` passes. Say how many tests ran.
2. `uv run whodunit casebook` has been rerun and the pages open.
3. The `hackathon.md` entry for the job is written.
4. Commit in small commits with messages in the style already in the log.
5. Read the new checkpoint with `entire checkpoint explain --transcript` and check it for keys, email addresses and anything from outside the repo other than the one approved clone. Tell me what you found.
6. Ask me before pushing. Tell me exactly what the push will publish.

## What to tell me at the end

One short message: which jobs are done, which are not and why, every number that changed in the README and where it comes from, what was spent on model calls, and anything I still have to do by hand before 11:55 PM.

### 6:00 PM, a case from one trace

Stage 2, fourth item. Until now a case file was written by hand: someone had to know the failing input, what it should have produced, and both ends of the range. `whodunit open-case --from-trace <id>` writes the file from one failing run and stops.

- It looks for the run in neatroots, and in neatlogs cloud if neatroots does not have it.
- The input is the root span's. The bad ref is the commit in the run_info tags.
- The expected result is what the nearest earlier run of the same input paid, among runs that passed. A run passed if it was not flagged and paid something different from the failing run.
- The good ref comes from `whodunit/onset.py`: every run of that input, judged against the expected result, goes through the same change-point model the lineup uses, and the range starts where that model is 99% sure nothing had gone wrong yet.
- If no earlier run passed, it asks one question: what should this request have produced? Away from a keyboard it prints the question, writes nothing and exits, and `--expect` gives the answer.
- A trace does not say how to build and run the agent, so that is copied from another case for the same agent.

Tried on the real traces, on an ordinary run from the traffic that refunded 30.00 on someone else's order. From the trace id alone it wrote a case with the right request, an expected result of no refund taken from a run 11 hours of traffic earlier, and a range of 41 suspects that holds the real culprit. That file went to a scratch folder and is not in `cases/`.

What it cannot do: the earlier runs of the same input are read from neatroots only. A trace that exists only in the cloud gets its input and its bad ref, and then has to be told the expected result and the good ref. And "passed" leans on neatroots' own flags, so a run that was wrong without being flagged, and wrong in a different way from the failing one, could be taken for the expected result. The file's first lines name the run the expectation came from, so a person can check it.

### 6:21 PM, when no commit did it
# Sealed eval, 11 October 2026

Five regressions were planted in the refund agent's history by a second coding session, through ordinary requests to fresh coding sessions. It wrote the answer key, and the key's SHA-256 was committed in 4c45f7f before Whodunit ran on any case. `eval/score.py` checks the key against that hash before scoring. The key was added to git only after every case had been run.

Replays ran on the hackathon gateway's small model, three at a time.

## Result

With 120 replays allowed per case: 3 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations, 2 cases where nobody was named.

The two open cases were then resumed from their own replays with up to 200 more allowed: 5 of 5 solved, 0 wrong accusations.

| Case | Rate the second session measured | Rate Whodunit estimated | At 120 replays | In the end | Replays | Commits replayed | Suspects |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| cents-off | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 21 | 5 | 13 |
| wrong-order-refunded | 30% | 12% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 9 | 12 |
| half-done-batch | 25% | 14% | nobody named | solved | 168 | 10 | 15 |
| strangers-paid | 72% | 59% | solved | solved | 30 | 5 | 11 |
| turned-away | 100% | 93% | solved | solved | 24 | 6 | 14 |

The rate Whodunit estimates is a posterior mean, so after only a few replays it sits below 100% even for a bug that fails every time.

## What it cost

Replay spend on the gateway, estimated from token counts at list prices, came to about $1.91 for all five cases:

- cents-off: about $0.08 (61,267 tokens)
- wrong-order-refunded: about $0.57 (438,034 tokens)
- half-done-batch: about $1.04 (795,110 tokens)
- strangers-paid: about $0.10 (78,530 tokens)
- turned-away: about $0.12 (100,111 tokens)

## What this does and does not show

- No commit was wrongly accused, at either budget. Five cases cannot show how often that would hold. The simulator puts a number on it for cases shaped like the two rare ones: with 320 replays allowed, about 4% of accusations name the wrong commit, and with 120 about 13%. See `eval/simulator/README.md`. On `half-done-batch` the top suspect at 120 replays was the wrong commit, at 53%, and Whodunit named nobody. That is the behaviour the 95% bar is for.
- The two cases it could not close at 120 replays are the two that fail least often. Whodunit put them at 12% and 14%, where the second session had measured 30% and 25% from a handful of probes. A bug that rare needs a lot of replays whatever the method.
- The ranges are short, 11 to 15 suspects. On ranges this size a careful scan from the oldest commit would have replayed about as many commits as Whodunit did, so this eval says little about savings on long histories. The simulator in `eval/simulator` covers 40 suspects.
- Five cases is a small sample. It is enough to say the pipeline works on a history it did not write, and not enough to put a number on accuracy.
- Each case has one planted regression inside its range, by design. Two regressions that touch the same inputs in one range are outside what the model assumes.

## What happened after the culprits were named

The owner's ruling was patch for all three kinds of change involved. A fix is kept when its failure rate is 95% likely to be back within 5 points of the rate before the culprit. The last column gives what the replays of the kept fix showed and the 95% upper bound on its failure rate. Clearing the bar is not proof: in simulation a fix that still fails 4 runs in 100 clears it about one time in three.

| Case | Outcome | Tries | Replays of the final fix, and the most it could still fail at 95% |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| cents-off | patch kept | 1 | 0 failures in 30, at most 6.2% |
| strangers-paid | patch kept | 1 | 0 failures in 30, at most 6.2% |
| wrong-order-refunded | patch kept | 1 | 0 failures in 36, at most 5.2% |
| turned-away | two patches fell short, then a revert was kept | 3 | 0 failures in 30, at most 6.2% |
| half-done-batch | not fixed | 3 | two patches left 5 failures in 90 each, at most 10.6%, and the revert conflicts |

So four of five were closed, one of them only by giving up on the patch the owner asked for, and one was left open and says so.

## The same culprit across the whole history

`cases/whole-history.toml` takes the `strangers-paid` regression and widens the range to the whole grown history, 57 suspects. With alibis from entire-graph for 22 of them and 18 ordinary runs as evidence, 20 replays across 5 commits named the culprit at 99.8%. A scan from the oldest suspect would have tested 37 commits. This is the run that speaks to savings on a longer history, and it is one run. Run again with no alibis and no ordinary runs to go on, it took 30 replays across 8 commits to reach 95.4%. So the head start saved 10 replays and 3 commits, in one run each way, with the two kinds of help taken away together.

Both runs were made again on Monday 12 October, from nothing. With the head start: 20 replays across 5 commits, 98.3%. Without it: 33 replays across 8 commits, 99.0%. That run also went on to the fix, and its first patch was rejected by the do-no-harm check. `cases/whole-history.casefile.html` has it.

### $NOW, Monday: the README says what broke before it says how

The owner had the repo read against the hackathon's rubric and brought back six findings. The first: a new reader cannot tell what Whodunit is for, because the README opens on a riddle and the outcome is four paragraphs down. This entry is that job.

- The README now opens with what the reader has (an agent that worked last week and now fails sometimes), what Whodunit tells them, and one case as a five-row table: what went wrong, which change, who asked for it, what it cost, the fix. The lineup screenshot is under it and links to the live page.
- A new section, "What it does on its own", walks the loop as eleven steps and points each at the record and key where it happened: \`whole-history\` for the lineup, motive, brief, remembered ruling, the patch thrown out and the patch kept, \`turned-away\` for the revert, \`half-done-batch\` for the case left open.
- A new "Evidence" table has one row per kind of evidence, with a link each. The three posts that are live are in it, and in \`evidence/README.md\`, which had listed them as missing.
- Everything that was in the README before is below those, word for word, except its first two paragraphs, which the new opening replaces.
- The casebook opens with the same sentence. Its old headline, "Which commit did it, and why.", is gone from the page, and the old lead is the second sentence of the new one. The serif italic word is now "sometimes."
- \`AGENTS.md\` has the new one-line pitch.

Numbers, each checked against \`cases/whole-history.record.json\`: 57 suspects, 98.3%, 20 replays across 5 commits, 22 alibis, 18 ordinary runs, 37 for a scan from the oldest, 11 of 14 runs, 4 of 4 lines from \`entire why\`, six brief sentences with none cut, 30 clean replays for each patch, 13 other requests with 54 and 42 replays, 8 of 8 against 5 of 8, 6.2%, 4 of 6 ordinary runs, 120.00, 176 replays, \$0.7999. The revert and the open case are from their own records: 5 of 12, 4 of 18, 0 of 30, and 5 of 90 twice.

Where the owner's draft and the records differed, the records won, and the owner was told:

- The draft said "one real case". The regression is one of the five a second session planted, so the word is gone and a paragraph under the table says what is real (the sessions, the request, the history) and what is staged (the regression, the customers).
- The draft said "about 80 cents". That is the replays alone. The model calls for the brief and the two patches are not in the record's count, so the line says "of replays".
- The draft said the first patch "broke another request". That request was already failing 5 times in 8. The line says it made another request fail more often, which is what the page says and what this log corrected once before.
- "11 minutes" holds as a round figure and from three places that do not quite agree because they time different things: 10 minutes 46 seconds in this log's entry for the run, 10 minutes 45 seconds on the neatlogs trace, and 10 minutes 39 seconds between the first and last replay in the record.
- No record in \`cases/\` was opened from a trace. The one time \`open-case --from-trace\` ran on real traffic, its file went to a scratch folder. Step 1 of the new section says so and points at this log.

Checked: 150 fast tests pass. The casebook was regenerated with the public address and its top was looked at in a browser at 800 px, where the headline takes two lines.

Not checked: the README as GitHub renders it, since nothing is pushed yet, and whether the table's last row wraps badly on a phone. The case pages themselves did not change.
